events.title: Harry Marlow's indenture torn at Cuan shean
events.body: Seumas Crùbach, shipwright of Cuan shean, takes down and tears the four-year indenture binding Harry Marlow to his yard, the guild court's charter rule having reached the coast that spring. He keeps Harry on the bench as a free hand rather than take a new bound apprentice in his place.

events.title: The Tuathaich day-wage set at the Cuan shean yard
events.body: Seumas Crùbach keeps Harry Marlow at half a bound man's wage and no guild standing once the indenture is loosed, a rate other yards along the coast take up that spring for the Tuathaich hands they keep on without a guild's leave to teach them.

events.title: A Tuathaich boy's plea refused at the Ros dhomhain guild court
events.body: A rope-maker's apprentice of four years' standing at Ros dhomhain brings his case to the newly chartered guild court and is heard and refused in a single sitting, the court ruling that the charter's custom of binding names Dia-thìrich hands alone.

events.title: The Moot's letter on the indentures filed
events.body: The Moot at Caol mhòr writes to the guild court at Cathair dhearg asking what is to become of the Tuathaich indentures already standing when the guilds' charters are read. The letter is filed among that year's business without an answer.

events.title: The lamp-makers' mark first stamped
events.body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, chartered that winter, set their mark, a flame struck over a hammer, on every coal lamp leaving their sheds from that year on, so that the lamp itself carries the record of where it was made and under what oath.

events.title: The chandlers' patrol-boat right first exercised
events.body: The newly chartered chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh fit out the Crown's patrol boats under their sole right that spring, and the fitting-out becomes the guild's yearly show of its charter before the shire's maor.

events.title: Harry Marlow measures the old wreck at Cuan shean
events.body: Freed from bound hours by the loosing of his indenture, Harry Marlow spends the year's stolen hours setting down in his own book the full lines of a derelict human hull left on the Cuan shean hard, learning by his own measure how a hull built plank first and framed after is made to hold together.

events.title: A northern passage offered and refused at Cuan shean
events.body: A cloth trader out of Seann Vell, putting in at Cuan shean that autumn, tells Harry Marlow a free hand might do better in a northern harbour, where no guild court stands over a craftsman's work. Harry thanks him and stays at his bench.

events.title: Harry Marlow sends his wage north at half rate
events.body: At the year's end Harry Marlow sends north to his father Joseph Marlow's forge at Doire mhin the sum he has set aside from a free hand's half-wage, a smaller sum than any year of his bound apprenticeship, kept from the same habit regardless.

events.title: Baile chiar's weavers take a guild charter
events.body: The council's clerks cut a new seal, a shuttle over a fleece, for the weavers of Baile chiar, entering the grant in a book bound in calf at Cathair dhearg after a fee is paid and a feast given. It is a charter of the ordinary kind: coin changes hands, a form is followed, and a craft already practised becomes a craft the kingdom has agreed to notice.

events.title: The Moot votes its school purse
events.body: The Moot at Caol mhòr sets aside money of its own for a schoolroom at Doire ghlas, without asking the council's leave a second time, Walter Hale having judged that a council which says no once will say no as often as it is asked.

events.title: A widow lends her byre at Doire ghlas
events.body: Jenny Marrow, whose husband's cattle a fever and a wet spring had thinned to a few head, offers her byre for the winter months in exchange for nothing but a promise that she and the children will be taught to write their names.

events.title: Walter Hale carries the school purse north
events.body: Walter Hale rides the coast road himself to bring Agnes Pike the Moot's money the evening before her school opens, and leaves with it a sheet in his own hand setting out that the purse is the Moot's, the room the widow's, and the leave nobody's at all.

events.title: Agnes Pike's school opens on the fourteenth of am Faoilleach
events.body: Eleven children come through the byre door at Doire ghlas before the Church bell finishes its stroke, to be taught their letters from the Bible and from a lent volume of the Moot's own minutes, there being no primer printed for the humans' tongue on the island.

events.title: The school's register begun
events.body: Agnes Pike opens a register for the byre school in its first week, its first leaf recording eleven scholars and that no leave was asked for the room because none was thought likely to be given.

events.title: Daniel Frayne walks in from Muileann leathan
events.body: A fisherman's son of nine walks the coast path each morning from Muileann leathan to sit on Agnes Pike's benches, and back again in time to help haul his father's nets, a condition he keeps every day the school runs that winter.

events.title: Daniel Frayne's fair copies pinned to the byre wall
events.body: Slower at reading than at writing, the boy is set to copy out each day's psalm or minute a second time, and by the spring his fair copies, stroke for stroke exact, are pinned the length of the byre's one dry wall.

events.title: The maor visits the byre school and writes nothing
events.body: The shire's maor, whose office is to note anything newly opened in it, rides out, watches the children recite a psalm, asks Agnes Pike only after the room's heating and the children's fees, and sends south that season a report of harvest, head-due and bridge that says nothing of the school at all.

events.title: Alice Hale opens a second school at Caol mhòr
events.body: Walter Hale's daughter Alice opens a school of her own in a disused net-store behind the harbour at Caol mhòr, on a purse thinner than her father carried north, and writes to Agnes Pike asking what has answered best on the byre's cold mornings.

events.title: The Cill ghlas fault line walked and found unmoved
events.body: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin and his chainman Iain mac Ruairidh trace the old Cill ghlas fault foot by foot with plumb and cord and file a report at Cathair mhòr declaring the district safe to work again so long as new shafts are cut a full chain back from it.

events.title: The school moves to the church porch for summer
events.body: With the widow's cattle wanting the byre back for the warm months, Agnes Pike's school moves into the porch of the Doire ghlas church, a change it makes every summer after.

events.title: Daniel Frayne copies the minute of the school's own founding
events.body: On the last morning before the move to the church porch, Agnes Pike sets her best copyist the Moot's own four-line minute recording the school's opening, and pins his fair copy into the register's first leaf rather than to the drying wall.

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid opens the Ceann mhòr assize
events.body: In the heat of an t-Iuchar, with the windows of the old magistrate's house propped open against the fish-yard smell, Eilidh nic Leòid tells the crowded room that she will hear all nineteen causes on the list to their own ends, in their own order, whatever the likeness of one paper to the next, and whatever the weather asks of everyone waiting on the bench.

events.title: The Dunlop title read to its end
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid reads a human grant brown at its folds, and a receipt for seed corn the family thought to bring unasked, and finds as she found seven years before at Seann Bhral: the ground is the Crown's, the working of it the Dunlops', on the same terms as before and no excusal from any due to come.

events.title: Fifteen suits found for the Crown at Ceann mhòr
events.body: Cause after cause of the seventeen brought on human titles is decided in the words of the Leòid ruling, the ground passing to the Crown and the working of it staying with the family that holds it, until the room has learned, before the week is out, to stop guessing at an ending it already knows.

events.title: A custodian's countersign found on the Coombe title
events.body: In the margin of a Tuathaich family's human grant, Eilidh nic Leòid finds the pressed mark of an old land-keeping custodian, witness to the transfer in the humans' own time, and rules that a grant allowed also by an office of the island's own older law stands on ground the crossing never touched.

events.title: The Coombes and the Pettifers found for the holders
events.body: Two of the seventeen suits at Ceann mhòr, each carrying a custodian's old countersign on its title, are found whole for the families that hold them, the only two of the assize's nineteen causes decided against the Crown that summer.

events.title: Walter Hale heard as a witness at Ceann mhòr
events.body: Having no standing to plead, Walter Hale is called instead to the bench as a witness, and shows Eilidh nic Leòid the Moot's own minute of a family's land divided by agreement and set down in writing years before, which the court accepts over the memory of the parties themselves.

events.title: The Moot's minute-books credited by a Crown bench
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid rules that a record kept by a body the Crown does not recognise is no less a fact for the hand that wrote it holding no seal, the first time the Moot's own paper is taken as evidence before a circuit justice.

events.title: Hale and Eilidh nic Leòid speak at the Ceann mhòr inn
events.body: Over supper Walter Hale asks Eilidh nic Leòid whether an exact law can also be a fair one; she tells him plainly that she made her ruling to be exact rather than kind, and that she knows whose convenience it was written to serve, a thing she has told no maor and no council chest.

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid begins the gathered book
events.body: Through the winter after the Ceann mhòr sitting, Eilidh nic Leòid sets down in one book the whole of her nine years' rulings on Tuathaich land, from the Seann Bhral ruling to the seventeen suits, so that a justice after her need not dig the council's own chests to learn what she already knows.

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid sends for Uilleam mac Leòid
events.body: Failing through am Màrt, Eilidh nic Leòid sends word north to her brother's son Uilleam, a young man who has ridden the northern circuit with her twice as a boy, asking him to take up the circuit she can no longer ride.

events.title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain
events.body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies in her own house within sound of the harbour, her clerk Murchadh Clàrc beside her and the gathered book of her rulings finished but not yet bound on the table by the bed.

events.title: Leabhar nam Breith bound
events.body: The council's own binder binds Eilidh nic Leòid's gathered rulings in plain calf under the name she chose for it herself, Leabhar nam Breith, and every circuit justice after her is given a copy to carry.

events.title: Uilleam mac Leòid named to the northern circuit
events.body: Uilleam mac Leòid is named circuit justice of the north in his aunt's place, and rides for his first assize with Leabhar nam Breith strapped behind his clerk's saddle, as the satchel of blank record-books was once strapped behind his aunt's.
